items.title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
items.summary: Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday.
items.body: The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist. Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates. Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.

items.title: This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it
items.summary: Janus Henderson portfolio manager John Lloyd, whose fund owns CoreWeave bonds, sees a buying opportunity for this 'best in class' data center play.
items.body: That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson. "It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity. Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund . The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. "Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

items.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
items.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look a possible mega-merger.
items.body: Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday. While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to consider it. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

items.title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
items.summary: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money Business live – latest updates An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving…
items.body: An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut . Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”. The US tech company said services were starting to come back online as of 1pm London time, and were back online for most customers by 3pm, but not before critical financial transactions and legal proceedings were disrupted. That included the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales, which failed to work throughout the morning.

items.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
items.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.
items.body: What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands. Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors. Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion. "From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

items.title: Frank Elderson: Interview with Die Presse
items.body: Almost without exception, banks complain about the high cost of regulation. Do they have a point? Or are these costs essential for the stability of the banking system? We shouldn’t forget the financial crisis of 2008. The costs were enormous, not only for banks, but also for households, firms, taxpayers and society as a whole. Those costs far outweigh the cost of regulation. The regulatory reforms introduced after the crisis have made European banks far more resilient. Banks today are well capitalised, have high liquidity levels and are more profitable, on average, than for many years. But wouldn’t it be possible to simplify supervision without putting the stability of the sector at risk? It’s true that regulation and the supervisory framework have become more complex over time.

items.title: ‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
items.summary: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging…
items.body: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter. A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks. Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.

items.title: Oil prices fall as traders hope for diplomatic progress in Middle East
items.summary: Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks.
items.body: Crude oil prices fell Tuesday as traders hoped for diplomatic progress between the U.S. and Iran, though attacks on tankers and strikes against Saudi Arabia have escalated recently. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November fell 1.8% to close at $101.79 per barrel, pulling back dramatically from a session high of $110.48. The November contract expired on Tuesday. The WTI December contract was down 26 cents at $98.28 per barrel. Global benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery fell 0.7% to settle at $108.79 per barrel, well off a session high of $111.99. Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks. At least 18 vessels have come under fire over the past two weeks, according to ship tracker Kpler.

items.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
items.summary: Revolut was one of the hardest hit, with banking services going down for many customers.
items.body: Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts. The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday. Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online. The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience. "We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

items.title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling
items.summary: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials What does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea…
items.body: The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs. Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments. The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it. It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.

items.title: China’s hybrid car exports to EU surge by more than 200% as import cap looms
items.summary: China’s hybrid car exports to the European Union tripled in September from a year earlier, with shipments expected to remain elevated before an import cap agreed during recent trade talks takes effect. The country shipped nearly 100,000 hybrid cars to the bloc last month, up…
items.body: China’s hybrid car exports to the European Union tripled in September from a year earlier, with shipments expected to remain elevated before an import cap agreed during recent trade talks takes effect. The country shipped nearly 100,000 hybrid cars to the bloc last month, up 18.9 per cent from August and 204.2 per cent from a year earlier, customs data showed on Tuesday. The surge outpaced a 142.7 per cent year-on-year rise in China’s total exports of passenger cars to the EU. Analysts said the rapid growth likely reflected carmakers front-loading vehicles ahead of high-level negotiations held in Beijing in early October. “Dealerships may have sought to get as many purchases in as possible before potential quotas or tariffs ahead of trade talks,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING.

items.title: Netflix posts third-quarter earnings beat, but shares fall on advertising and revenue guidance
items.summary: Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes
items.body: Netflix on Tuesday reported third-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates and revenue that was in line as Wall Street eyes the company's engagement and advertising metrics. The streamer's revenue was almost 12% higher year over year, boosted by growth in membership and an increase in subscription prices that went into effect in March, the company said. Netflix said the response to those price hikes has been consistent with prior changes and with its expectations. Net income for the quarter was $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, compared with $2.55 billion, or 59 cents a share in the same period last year. Netflix said the year-over-year jump in profit was due in part to the timing of expenses. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise more than 11% to $13.44 billion, driven by growth in memberships, pricing and ad revenue, it said.

items.title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
items.summary: The long-awaited decision about the controversial North Sea field is expected on Wednesday morning.
items.body: The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made. The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months. Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.

items.title: NatWest cracks down on 13,000 staff attending office two days a month
items.summary: Union furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a week NatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union. The banking group,…
items.body: NatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union. The banking group, which serves customers under the Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands, will require all of its nearly 40,000 UK staff to follow a strict two days a week office schedule from February 2027, abolishing a remote-first policy for thousands of employees. Unite said it was a “kick in the teeth” for the 13,000 employees who attend the office only two days a month, and accounted for some of NatWest’s lowest-paid workers, including staff involved in technology, security, data analytics and human resources. The union said the change would pile additional financial pressure on staff already struggling with rising living costs, while undermining flexible arrangements for those with caring responsibilities or disabilities.

items.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
items.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
items.body: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies. The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August. The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers. The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses". Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada.

items.title: Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7% as John Healey’s first budget looms
items.summary: Latest ONS data presents mixed picture amid slump in job vacancies and analysts warning labour market is ‘running on idle’ Business live – news updates Healey to reject calls to raise CGT in budget Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs…
items.body: Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs market before John Healey’s first budget next week. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics . City economists had forecast a rise to 5%. In a further boost to the chancellor, the figures also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3 million. However, a slump in the number of job vacancies illustrated what some economists said was an economy moving sideways. After hitting a peak of 1.3m in the period after the pandemic, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic.

items.title: Chinese carmakers gear up European production to sidestep tariffs, import quota
items.summary: Chinese carmakers, facing a European Union import quota targeting their hybrid electric vehicles (EVs), are gearing up for more local production to reinforce their go-global drive. They plan to either splash out billions of yuan to set up their own factories or tap international…
items.body: Chinese carmakers, facing a European Union import quota targeting their hybrid electric vehicles (EVs), are gearing up for more local production to reinforce their go-global drive. They plan to either splash out billions of yuan to set up their own factories or tap international marques’ idle plants to build their vehicles, looking to sustain a sales boom in one of the world’s major automotive markets. “Global growth shifts from exporting vehicles to Europe to producing them locally, from price-led market share gains to margin-led positioning, and from a single export channel to a multimarket footprint,” Morgan Stanley analysts said in a research note issued last week after Beijing and Brussels agreed on an import quota for Chinese-made hybrid vehicles.

items.title: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests
items.summary: Protests broke out in France and several European countries as people railed against living costs, poor schooling conditions, and a housing crisis.
items.body: Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities. France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers. Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent. There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC.

items.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
items.summary: No formal investigation has started, but the regulator is making inquiries into the case.
items.body: The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City. The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September. No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case. It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than £900m. City are appealing the verdict. The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations.

items.title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts
items.summary: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by…
items.body: Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict. Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%. “You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe , I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 ​months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels. Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs.

items.title: Beijing warns London of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it aligns with EU import curbs on EVs
items.summary: As London considers aligning with EU trade measures targeting imports of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), Beijing has warned of “firm countermeasures” if the UK imposes restrictions. “We hope the UK will abide by World Trade Organization rules and think twice before acting,…
items.body: As London considers aligning with EU trade measures targeting imports of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), Beijing has warned of “firm countermeasures” if the UK imposes restrictions. “We hope the UK will abide by World Trade Organization rules and think twice before acting, rather than blindly following the EU,” the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. “China will closely monitor developments and take firm countermeasures if the UK insists on restricting Chinese electric vehicles.” The ministry’s statement was in response to remarks last week by Anas Sarwar, the United Kingdom’s trade minister, who said Britain and the European Union must “work together and act in lockstep” to address China’s dominance in the automotive sector. The British government was continuing discussions with the EU on potential tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, he said.

items.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
items.summary: The government increased taxes on online casino and sports betting in last year's Budget.
items.body: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry. Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed. The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year. Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market". "We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday.

items.title: September data shows housing market in a deep freeze
items.summary: New data on the housing market's performance in September is bleak, with sales, construction and sentiment all falling more than expected.
items.body: Fast-rising mortgage rates in September took a harsh toll on the housing market, according to new monthly data released today. Pending home sales, a measure of signed contracts on existing homes, dropped 7.3% from August and were down 11.3% year-over-year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This count reflects buyers out shopping in September, when the average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose sharply. It started the month around 6.8% and hit 7.6% by the end of the month, according to Mortgage News Daily. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release. Regionally, sales dropped across the nation but the biggest month-to-month drops were in the South (-8.2%) and West (-9.2%).

items.title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
items.summary: The bank says workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week from February.
items.body: The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home. NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February. The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility. But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs. Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic. In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home.

items.title: Thames Water creditors secure former Labour minister to drive rescue deal
items.summary: Stricken UK water supplier lines up John Hutton as independent chair designate if takeover goes ahead The group of Thames Water creditors pursuing a £10bn rescue deal for Britain’s largest water supplier has lined up a former senior Labour minister to chair the company, as it…
items.body: The group of Thames Water creditors pursuing a £10bn rescue deal for Britain’s largest water supplier has lined up a former senior Labour minister to chair the company, as it tries to win over the government. The creditor consortium, called London & Valley Water, said on Tuesday that Lord John Hutton had been selected as independent chair designate of the Thames Water board, if the consortium’s deal is approved. Creditors have been locked in talks with ministers and regulators for months over the future ownership of the debt-laden water company, which has 16 million customers in the south of England. Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames and present him with more radical options for the stricken company, the Guardian reported this week . Before he became prime minister, he said he would nationalise Thames.

items.title: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT
items.summary: Democrats are hopeful that they will regain majority control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in November's elections.
items.body: Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections, The New York Times reported Tuesday, citing his team. Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, President Donald Trump , in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates. The dueling announcements came as Republicans are increasingly worried about retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress. Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate. Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times.

items.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
items.summary: Influential Labour figures had been pushing for equalising CGT and income tax, but critics have said this could drive wealthy people out of Britain.
items.body: Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times , external , Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences. The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets. If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

items.title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
items.summary: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday Business live – latest updates India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO),…
items.body: India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn. Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday. Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians. Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO.

items.title: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend
items.summary: France will deploy Sentinelle troops for Saturday's protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
items.body: France will deploy some military forces to help maintain order during a fresh wave of protests expected this weekend, officials said Tuesday. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in the National Assembly that the government would ⁠deploy forces from France's Sentinelle force — a domestic military operation that was launched in 2015 following terrorist attacks in Paris — "mainly on static security missions." This would free up police and gendarmes — a military police force — to carry out law enforcement objectives, Nuñez added.

items.title: French unrest, AI debt risks push investors toward ultralong JGBs
items.body: Police in riot gear stand guard in Paris as a fire burns. French government bond yields have risen amid political instability and concerns about the country's public finances. TOKYO -- Demand for ultralong-term Japanese government bonds proved brisk at an auction Tuesday of 20-year debt as uncertainty around French bonds and worries about artificial intelligence-related financial risk whet investors' appetite for assets seen as relatively safe.

items.summary: Entertainment giant shakes up creative leadership as viewership growth stalls and current quarter profits set to disappoint

items.title: The Social Security Administration corrected millions of records, and says there’s more to fix
items.summary: In an effort to thwart fraud, the Social Security Administration said it has fixed millions of records and is working on correcting millions more.

items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
items.summary: A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination.
items.body: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago. A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out. Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations. The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.

items.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders | Nils Pratley
items.summary: As long as Healey doesn’t go overboard, a small turn on surcharge dial will not seriously undermine flow of capital Everyone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less…
items.body: E veryone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity. In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week , the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to “stay the course” on the fiscal rules by finding some money from somewhere, tapping the banks is a reasonable policy. Or, at least, better than most alternatives.

items.title: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
items.summary: Anthropic and Nscale previously inked a similar deal for a data center on the same site in the U.S.
items.body: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The agreement would cover a second 460-megawatt data center at the same West Virginia site as the first deal, the person said. The person asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the talks. The deal could be worth around $45 billion, the person said. Bloomberg first reported that Anthropic and Nscale were in talks over a second deal. Anthropic declined to comment. Nscale has been approached for comment. Nvidia -backed Nscale is one of several companies that have emerged in recent years to develop the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence. The company builds or leases data centers and sells computing capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs.

items.title: Japan PM's party pushes to fast-track debate on food tax cut
items.body: TOKYO -- A proposed tax cut on food is expected to undergo unusually swift deliberations in Japan's parliament, compared with past changes to one of the country's most important revenue sources.

items.title: Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
items.summary: Small firms cite labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring, the Office for National Statistics says.
items.body: The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year. However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring.

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions…
items.body: A utonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center . In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising.

items.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks
items.summary: The U.K.'s Royal Air Force will deploy jets to assist with defensive operations, but will not engage in offensive strikes.
items.body: The U.K. said it would provide defensive military support, including fighter jets, to support Saudi Arabia as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalate. The Houthis, a Yemeni militant group, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets in recent weeks. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage, while facilities belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco were targeted last week. "The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region," U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement on Tuesday. He added that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles.

items.title: Japan offers opportunities, partnerships for defense contractor Thales: CEO
items.body: PARIS -- French defense and technology group Thales sees "a lot of potential opportunities to grow" its business in Japan and for partnerships with Japanese companies, as the country expands its defense industry, CEO Patrice Caine told Nikkei at the company's headquarters outside Paris.

items.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
items.summary: The changes come after concerns that penalties issued by private providers are too harsh and leave motorists unfairly punished.
items.body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished. The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty. Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong. Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded.

items.title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
items.summary: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve…
items.body: A nother morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.

items.title: Zelenskyy to meet with U.S. envoy as tensions with Trump mount
items.summary: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to meet with U.S. special envoys on Tuesday after President Donald Trump aimed fresh criticism at the wartime leader.
items.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to meet with U.S. special envoys on Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump aimed a fresh spate of criticism at the wartime leader. Zelenskyy will arrive in Norway on Tuesday and meet with the country's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr and President of Finland Alexander Stubb in Oslo later in the day. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also take part in the discussions. The meetings come as tensions mount between Zelenskyy and Trump, while the U.S. has recently eased some pressure on Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine requested that Witkoff and Kushner join the meeting in Oslo, Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement. "Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries, and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work.

items.title: Toyota to build hydrogen-powered Hilux pickup in Thailand
items.body: BANGKOK -- Toyota Motor plans to begin Thai production of a hydrogen fuel cell version of its Hilux pickup truck in December 2027, initially for export.

items.title: 'I'm fed up of swiping': The singles choosing dating events over apps
items.summary: The BBC hears from people who think dating events are better value for money than dating apps.
items.body: Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on.

items.title: Is this the beginning of the end of the AI stock market boom?
items.summary: After a wobble on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under way Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this…
items.body: The world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this year’s estimated $US1tn investment in artificial intelligence is resting on a castle made of sand. Last week, the Nasdaq 100 – an index of the 100 biggest non-financial stocks on the American tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange – dropped by 5.5%, triggering the usual angst that the AI boom is about to go bust. The recent rot may have started with the failure of Firmus, an Australian datacentre company, to list on the ASX. The multi-billion dollar initial public offering was, at one stage, on track to make Firmus worth more than Telstra – even before having delivered on its promised earnings. That proved to be a fever dream of its founders and a wake-up call to investors in Australia and around the world to reconsider the potential value of similar businesses.

items.title: If Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catch
items.summary: Elon Musk's planned SpaceX stock donation could come with strings attached if he uses Trump Accounts. New Treasury rules limit when shares can be sold.
items.body: Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X . Posts from the White House and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also referenced Musk's gift as benefiting Trump Accounts. But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached. Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble.

items.title: Japan eyes private-sector H3 launches to compete with SpaceX
items.body: TOKYO -- Japan plans to begin discussions with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries on transferring responsibility to the company for launch operations of the country's flagship H3 rocket, looking to complete the transition by 2027.

items.title: Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?
items.summary: Around one in eight 16- to 24-year-olds are ‘Neet’ – and Alan Milburn is hinting that the overhaul of their support may be controversial With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have…
items.body: With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have signalled that welfare benefits may be cut to fund more job support for them. What may change and who will be affected? Ministers are expected to make a major policy announcement in November on plans to tackle what has been called a “generational challenge” and a “moral crisis” – the persistent number of young people in the UK who are out of work, not in college or training, or economically inactive . The head of the government-commissioned review of young people and work , Alan Milburn, has been vigorously preparing the ground in media interviews for what he has hinted will be a major – and potentially controversial – overhaul of employment and benefits support for young people.

items.title: Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 51%
items.summary: The company's latest acquisition is expected to close in fiscal 2028, and will see Braze shareholders receive $47.50 in cash per share.
items.body: Salesforce announced an agreement Tuesday to buy customer engagement platform Braze in a deal worth about $5.66 billion. Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share. Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The transaction is expected to close in fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, according to a Salesforce blog . The stock skyrocketed more than 51% on Tuesday to close at $45.57 after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging. "Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement.

items.title: Polaris to launch $630m private credit fund, one of Japan's largest
items.body: TOKYO -- Japanese investment fund Polaris Capital Group is set, by the end of fiscal 2026 at the earliest, to launch a private credit fund that will be one of the largest in the country, aiming to raise about 100 billion yen ($630 million) in capital from institutional investors, including life insurers and pension funds, Nikkei has learned.

items.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
items.summary: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.
items.body: President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households. The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up. So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.

items.title: Why have countries been pushing for a vital global climate report to be delayed?
items.summary: Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC review The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suspended an important meeting on Friday in Addis Ababa without setting out a firm timetable for its next report. The world’s…
items.body: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suspended an important meeting on Friday in Addis Ababa without setting out a firm timetable for its next report. The world’s governments are due to meet in less than a month for the Cop31 climate summit, and this leaves the future of scientific advice to governments on the climate in doubt . The IPCC – the UN-convened body of the world’s leading climate scientists – met for a week but, despite progress in many areas, was unable to come to agreement on the substantive issue of setting a launch date for its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of climate science. The seventh assessment report, known as AR7, was expected to be published in 2028, seven years after the last report in 2021 . But some want this timetable to be delayed to 2029, or later.

items.title: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis
items.summary: Novo released new evidence that its experimental CagriSema injection can improve upon the weight loss with its blockbuster GLP-1 obesity injection, Wegovy.
items.body: Novo on Tuesday said its next-generation obesity drug, CagriSema, showed 25% weight loss on average among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. The Danish company said further work is needed to confirm the hypotheses of two post-study analyses. Still, the results are the latest evidence that the experimental injection can improve upon the weight loss and other benefits offered by Novo's GLP-1 drug semaglutide, the active ingredient in its blockbuster obesity shot Wegovy and diabetes counterpart Ozempic. CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and another drug called cagrilintide that targets the amylin pathway, is expected to launch early next year.

items.title: Mynt, Philippine digital wallet GCash parent, goes public in Manila
items.body: MANILA -- Fintech company Mynt, the parent of popular digital wallet GCash, listed on the Philippine Stock Exchange on Tuesday, marking the largest initial public offering in the country at 60.9 billion pesos ($965 million).

items.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
items.summary: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".
items.body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France . The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting". Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend. "The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said. Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

items.title: Do not be distracted by global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now | Steven Guilbeault
items.summary: In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action When I was five, property developers came to cut down the…
items.body: W hen I was five, property developers came to cut down the woods behind my home in La Tuque, Quebec. My mother encouraged me to climb one of the trees in protest, then told the developers, straight-faced, that there was nothing she could do when they asked her to get me down. A few days later, the tree was cut down anyway. I thought about that tree in the early hours of a freezing Montreal morning in December 2022, as the gavel came down on a global agreement between nearly 200 countries to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. I thought about how important nature is for our health, our food security and our economies, but also how much passion there is around protecting it, and how it has the power to inspire people all around the world.

items.title: Apple adds U.S. titanium supplier for iPhone Duo as supply stays tight
items.summary: Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro.
items.body: Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro as part of a push to expand manufacturing in its home country. The company said Tuesday it will commit up to $100 million over the next three years to Perryman Company, based in Houston, Pennsylvania, for the production of titanium used in Apple products, including the $1,999 foldable Duo. Since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, Apple has been vocal about its efforts to invest more in the U.S., even as the final assembly of most iPhones remains overseas. In August of last year, Apple launched the American Manufacturing Program (AMP), increasing its plan for domestic spending by $100 billion to a total of $600 billion.

items.title: China's Chery eyes hybrid vehicle launch in Japan amid trade barriers
items.body: WUHU, China -- Chinese carmaker Chery Automobile plans to launch a hybrid vehicle in Japan next year, following rival BYD into the competitive Japanese market.

items.title: ‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’
items.summary: Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong After Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed…
items.body: A fter Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed the parcel arrived empty. Warrilow, 47, from Oxford, provided Vinted with photos and videos of the package, including date-stamped Ring doorbell footage of her leaving the house to post it. But she says the resale platform refunded the buyer and left her out of pocket. “I challenged Vinted on what evidence they had and asked them to supply it, but they simply said ‘based on our evidence’ and ‘our evidence suggests’ and could not explain what that was,” she says. “The photos from the buyer showed that all of the parcel tape I’d used had been removed.” Vinted has become a giant of the secondhand economy.

items.title: What options traders expect from SpaceX earnings after the bell
items.summary: It's been a busy three months for SpaceX. Traders think that means more gains for the stock after it reports earnings after the bell today.
items.body: The company delivered four astronauts to the International Space Station in record time, expanded its mobile network spectrum, is reportedly eyeing a $40 billion debt deal to buy Nvidia chips, and CEO Elon Musk said he plans to give shares to every kid in America next year. Traders think all that means more gains for the stock after it reports earnings after the bell Tuesday. Options market-makers are pricing about a 6% swing for SpaceX after the event, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's less than half the 13% it erased after its inaugural report in August, a selloff that turned out to be the low for the shares, which rallied 60% the following two months before reversing before dropping as much as 19% the past two weeks. While there are about as many open call contracts as puts on the stock, daily trading volume has leaned toward calls the past week, Barchart data shows.

items.title: Asia's AI boom is benefiting business owners, not consumers, economists say
items.body: BANGKOK -- The ongoing artificial intelligence investment boom in Asia is lifting exports and economic growth, but the benefits are not filtering down to consumers, economists said at a luxury business conference on Tuesday.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting bug had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
items.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, who is accused of planting a recording device, has been denied bail.
items.body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing , external in California. US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest. The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial. Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder. The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

items.title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show
items.summary: These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas? Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the…
items.body: These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas? W ho knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell? To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other.

items.title: Stock investors are ready to move on from the AI rout. Credit investors are not
items.summary: Investors were still demanding high yields and more insurance on CoreWeave and Oracle bonds.
items.body: AI stocks rallied on Monday, but CoreWeave closed slightly lower as investors remained skittish about its debt. Yields on Oracle debt also remained elevated as credit worries persist across the AI trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gained 1% on Monday. Oracle rose 1% after dropping 9% last week, while Intel climbed 2.4%, Advanced Micro Devices added 1.8 % and Micron Technology rose 3%. CoreWeave , the so-called neocloud company that led the sell-off last week, bounced around, hit a 52-week low and ultimately closed fractionally lower. Meanwhile, its bond yields remained high and its five-year credit default swaps were at distressed levels. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 was at 14.9%, slightly down from its high of over 15% last week. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps stood at roughly 1,082 basis points, nearly 2% lower than Friday.

items.title: Japan's Zipair launches Kuala Lumpur flight as first Malaysia route
items.body: NARITA, Japan -- Japanese budget carrier Zipair Tokyo launched a new route from Narita International Airport near Tokyo to the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur, on Tuesday, aiming to capture a wide range of demand beyond business and leisure travel.

items.title: ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.summary: Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile…
items.body: T he cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze. In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves. Delgado’s milk production has fallen by half. As the dry season approaches, he is selling off cattle for fear of what is to come.

items.title: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance
items.summary: GM narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its adjusted automotive free cash flow outlook after beating Wall Street’s third-quarter estimates.
items.body: DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations. The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program. Despite the positive news, GM stock fell nearly 7% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations. Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.

items.title: £30 rise in payments for crisis-hit households
items.summary: More money is made available through a resilience fund for hard-pressed households in Sheffield.
items.body: Crisis payments for people in Sheffield who are facing severe financial difficulties have been raised by £30. Single person households which qualify for help from Sheffield City Council's crisis and resilience fund will now be entitled to a one-off payment of £95, up from £65 previously. Meanwhile, two-person households can apply for a payment of £110, while homes with three or four people are entitled to £120 if they qualify and households with five or more people can get £130, the authority confirmed. Announcing the change, councillor Elle Dodd, chair of the authority's finance and performance policy committee, said life was "difficult and expensive" for "too many people" in Sheffield. The fund can be used to help people buy essentials such as food, toiletries and utilities, the council's website stated.

items.title: DIY repair clubs are helping Americans save money and fight big tech
items.summary: US community repair clinics teach people how to fix their belongings, pushing back against throwaway culture On a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York . Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit…
items.body: O n a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York . Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit boards at a workbench. Caleb Young, a co-founder of the Brooklyn Spark space, fit a DIY suction device on to the handle of a Dyson vacuum cleaner. “It’s in our culture to throw things away, but sometimes the fix is easier than you’d think,” Young said. The Fixit Clinic is open every Monday night to walk-ins. Anyone with a broken item they’d like to fix – from torn clothes to malfunctioning electronic devices – can drop by during open hours and get the repair help and tools they need. It’s a way for people to push back against tech companies, making their phones and gadgets deliberately unrepairable so they buy newer devices while creating large amounts of e-waste .

items.title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel
items.summary: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival Museums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so…
items.body: M useums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling. “There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder of Carmody Groarke , the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firms Atama and Re-st .

items.title: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet
items.summary: Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing.
items.body: AI is a transformational technology worth investing in — but investors must be selective when investing in data centers, according to the head of one of the world's biggest banks. Speaking to CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery called artificial intelligence "a major enabler to re-engineer and reimagine all our businesses, all our activities." "It's going to put a lot of power back in the hands of our colleagues because of the level of productivity it gives them, so it's going to be transformational, and we're certainly very much on a journey to adopt it," he said, adding that AI would help to "re-engineer the bank." But when it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, he advised discernment over an all-in approach. "One has to be selective," Elhedery said.
